title: The promise
narration: Here’s the whole idea. Most UI tests fail because a selector moved, not because the product is broken. Intent QA stores what the user is trying to do, and what must remain true. It can recover a harmless interaction change, but it will not rewrite an assertion or explain away a real bug. Let me show you the entire developer experience, from a clean checkout to the correctness boundaries.

title: Install and validate
narration: I’m starting from a clean clone. Installation is ordinary npm: install the dependencies, initialize the QA workspace, and validate it. Init is idempotent, so it creates anything missing without overwriting an edit. Validation applies the schemas and the cross-file checks before we spend time opening a browser. A spec list confirms the repository is ready.

title: Create semantic QA
narration: Now I create a test from a normal requirement. I choose the local environment, reuse the login fixture, and state the visible outcome I care about. The result is editable YAML. Notice what is not here: no CSS selector, XPath, coordinate, or fixed sleep. The intent and expectation are the source of truth, and the CLI and workspace UI validate and save the exact same file.

title: Run the real journey
narration: For execution, I ask the autonomous QA skill to run checkout card on local. This is the important boundary: Codex drives the real app through its native Browser capability. The reusable fixture signs in, the agent opens the cart, reaches checkout, submits the approved test payment, and observes the confirmation. The workspace picks up the completed file-backed result automatically. Every step passed, the accessible targets are recorded, and the screenshots explain the decision.

title: Heal harmless drift
narration: Now I change the application, not the test. Proceed to checkout moves into a menu and becomes Continue to payment. I rerun the same spec with every expectation unchanged. The old target is gone, so the agent captures that failure, rediscovers one explicitly equivalent accessible control, retries once, and checks the original checkout-form expectation. It passes. That is a healed interaction, supported by before-and-after evidence—not an edited requirement.

title: Keep real bugs red
narration: Next, a real functional bug. The checkout interaction still works, but the application says the order could not be completed. There is nothing to heal: the action succeeded and the required outcome failed. The result stays a functional regression, and the original assertion still says that an order confirmation must be visible. This is the correctness guarantee—the agent never negotiates the expectation to manufacture a pass.

title: Detect design regression
narration: Finally, behavior succeeds but the approved design does not. The action appears before the heading, and the green success treatment becomes a red warning panel. Because the functional steps passed, the separate design checkpoint runs at its declared viewport. The result shows the explicit reference, the actual screenshot, and concrete order and style findings. That supports a design regression; it is not the agent grading the page by taste.

title: Inspectable correctness
narration: Everything remains inspectable. Specs, results, screenshots, and the last-run pointer are ordinary repository files, so the UI is optional. Ninety-seven tests enforce the path guards, atomic saves, immutable expectations, healing boundary, classification rules, design evidence, demo resets, and the localhost workspace. That is the complete loop: install, describe intent, run the native browser, recover harmless drift, and keep real regressions visible.
